tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# kitty — design
2	
3	## Intent
4	
5	A command-line tool for tracking shared expenses on group trips. The group
6	records who paid for what and any repayments between them. At the end of the
7	trip, `kitty` says who owes whom and suggests payments that square everyone up.
8	All reporting commands print JSON so the owner can script against them.
9	
10	## Goals
11	
12	- Run as `python3 -m kitty <command>` from the project folder, using only the
13	  Python standard library. Must work on **Python 3.9** (the owner's version):
14	  no `match`, no `X | Y` type unions at runtime.
15	- Keep all state in `kitty.json` in the current working directory.
16	- Money is exact. Nothing is lost or invented by rounding: an expense's shares
17	  always add up exactly to its base amount.
18	- Every user error (unknown member, bad amount, bad date, missing kitty, …)
19	  prints a message and exits with status 1. No tracebacks.
20	
21	## Non-goals
22	
23	- Editing entries in place. Mistakes are fixed by removing the entry and
24	  adding it again.
25	- Currencies with something other than two decimal places. Every amount is
26	  treated as having cents.
27	- Live exchange rates. Rates are whatever the user sets.
28	- A minimum-transfers settle algorithm. A simple greedy one is good enough.
29	
30	## Anti-goals
31	
32	- A later rate change silently altering balances that were already settled.
33	- A traceback or a partly written `kitty.json` when something goes wrong.
34	
35	## Approaches considered
36	
37	- **A. One file** (`kitty/__main__.py`). Quickest to write, but the rounding and
38	  settling rules get mixed in with argument parsing and file handling, which
39	  makes them hard to test on their own.
40	- **B. A small package of plain functions (chosen).** Separate modules for
41	  parsing money and dates, splitting, storage, the calculations, and the CLI.
42	  The calculations take the loaded data and return results, without doing any
43	  I/O, so each rule can be unit-tested directly.
44	- **C. A class-based model** (Kitty, Member, Expense, Payment classes saved to
45	  JSON). Adds code for turning objects into JSON and back, and the rules are no
46	  easier to test than in B.
47	
48	The owner picked B, with `unittest` for the tests.
49	
50	## Decided behaviour
51	
52	### Currencies and rates (owner's decision)
53	
54	- `init CODE` sets the base currency.
55	- `rate set CODE RATE` means 1 CODE = RATE base units. It replaces any earlier
56	  rate for that code.
57	- A rate is **locked when an expense or payment is recorded**: the entry stores
58	  the rate it used and its base amount. A later `rate set` only affects entries
59	  added after it.
60	- Using a currency that isn't the base currency and has no rate set is an
61	  error.
62	- To fix a mistake, remove the entry and add it again.
63	
64	### Members (owner's decisions)
65	
66	- Names are **case-insensitive**. "alice" and "Alice" are the same person.
67	  Adding "alice" when "Alice" exists is an error.
68	- Every command accepts any spelling of a name. Output always uses the name as
69	  it was first added.
70	- Names can't contain `,` or `=`.
71	- `member remove` is refused if the person appears in any expense (as payer or
72	  in its shares) or any payment.
73	- `member list` prints names in the order they joined.
74	
75	### Splitting (owner's decisions)
76	
77	- Shares are worked out in the **base currency** and saved when the expense is
78	  added.
79	- By default the cost is split equally among **everyone in the group at that
80	  moment**. People who join later aren't part of earlier splits.
81	- The payer doesn't have to be one of the people sharing the cost.
82	- At most one of `--among`, `--exact`, `--shares` and `--percent` can be used.
83	- **Equal splits** (default or `--among`): everyone gets
84	  `base_amount // n` cents. The leftover cents are handed out one at a time.
85	  For the default split, that goes in the order people joined. For `--among`, it
86	  goes in the order the names are given on the command line.
87	  Example: 10.00 split three ways is 3.34, 3.33, 3.33.
88	- **`--shares` and `--percent`:** each person gets their exact portion of the
89	  base amount rounded down to the cent. The leftover cents are then handed out
90	  one at a time, in command-line order.
91	- **`--exact`:** the amounts are in the expense's own currency and must add up
92	  exactly to the expense amount.
93	- `--percent` values must add up to exactly 100.
94	
95	### Settling up (owner's decisions)
96	
97	- At each step, the person who owes the most pays the person who is owed the
98	  most. The payment is the smaller of the two amounts. Repeat until everyone is
99	  at zero.
100	- When two people are tied, whoever comes first alphabetically (ignoring case)
101	  goes first.
102	- Payments are listed in the order they're worked out.
103	
104	### Balances
105	
106	A person's balance is:
107	
108	> what they paid for expenses − their shares + repayments they made −
109	> repayments they received
110	
111	It is positive if they're owed money and negative if they owe.
112	
113	### History
114	
115	- `history NAME` lists every expense the person paid for or had a share in,
116	  and every payment they made or received.
117	- Entries are sorted by date, then by the order they were added.
118	- Each entry shows its change to the person's balance and the running balance.
119	- Payments are described as "Payment to Alice" or "Payment from Bob".
120	
121	### Report
122	
123	`report` shows, per category, the sum of each person's **shares**, not what
124	they paid. Only people with a share in a category are listed under it.
125	
126	### Payments (owner's additions)
127	
128	- `payment add FROM TO AMOUNT [--currency C] [--date D]` records a repayment and
129	  prints its ID.
130	- `payment list` lists payments.
131	- `payment remove ID` deletes one.
132	- Payment IDs are numbered separately from expense IDs.
133	
134	### IDs and dates
135	
136	- IDs start at 1, count up, and are never reused, even after a removal.
137	- Dates must be real calendar dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. `2026-02-30` is an
138	  error. The default is today's local date.
139	
140	### Output formats (owner's)
141	
142	All JSON is printed with `json.dumps` defaults, giving one line with `", "`
143	and `": "` separators, exactly like the examples below. Money is a string with
144	two decimals, such as `"-20.70"` or `"0.00"`. It is in the base currency,
145	except for an expense's or payment's own `amount`.
146	
147	- `member list`: `["Alice", "Bob"]`
148	- `expense list`:
149	  `[{"id": 1, "date": "2026-07-14", "payer": "Alice", "description": "Dinner", "amount": "45.00", "currency": "USD", "base_amount": "41.40", "category": "food", "shares": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}]`
150	- `balances`: `{"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "-20.70"}`
151	- `settle`: `[{"from": "Bob", "to": "Alice", "amount": "20.70"}]`
152	- `history Bob`:
153	  `[{"date": "2026-07-14", "description": "Dinner", "change": "-20.70", "balance": "-20.70"}]`
154	- `report`: `{"food": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}`
155	- `export FILE` writes a CSV with the header
156	  `id,date,payer,description,amount,currency,category,base_amount`.
157	
158	## Calls made by the designer (owner may override)
159	
160	These weren't discussed. They are settled here so the builder doesn't have to
161	guess.
162	
163	1. **Converting `--exact` to the base currency.** The exact amounts are
164	   treated as weights, using the same rule as `--shares`. Each person gets
165	   `floor(exact_i × base_amount / amount)` cents, and the leftover cents are
166	   handed out in command-line order. In the base currency this gives exactly
167	   the amounts entered.
168	2. **Base amount** = amount × rate, rounded half-up to the cent.
169	3. **Amounts** must be greater than 0 and have at most two decimal places.
170	   `45`, `45.5` and `45.50` are all valid. Things like `0`, `-5`, `1e3`, `1,000`,
171	   `nan` and `abc` are errors. The same rules apply to `--exact` values.
172	4. **Share and percent values** must be positive decimal numbers. Fractional
173	   values like `33.5` are allowed.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
